canonical_topic: Basis for testing hedge effectiveness: changes in value, not levels
definition: A hedge is effective when a $1 move in the hedged item's price is matched by a roughly $1 offsetting move in the hedge's value. Because of this, effectiveness testing compares period-to-period changes in value between the hedge and the hedged item, not their absolute price levels.
core_idea: Hedge quality is judged by how closely the day-to-day value changes of the hedge track the day-to-day value changes of the hedged item, rather than by comparing the two items' price levels directly.
key_points: The ideal hedge offsets the hedged item's value change roughly dollar-for-dollar.
Effectiveness tests use day-to-day (or period-to-period) changes in value, not the values themselves.
This distinction matters because comparing raw price levels would not reveal whether the two positions move together.
relationships: Feeds into regression-based effectiveness tests (slope, R-squared) described in the same section.
trading_implications: When building a hedge test, prepare a changes-in-value (or percent-change) series for both instruments before running any statistical analysis.
caveats: Assuming hedge effectiveness can be judged by comparing the two items' price levels rather than their changes in value.
